Part 1 · Why we vote at all
01Direct, and indirectSeven offices, and who actually does the choosing35 XP

Representatives can be chosen through direct or indirect elections. Slide through the seven offices and watch the chain change length.

Chosen by
—
Electoral system
—
Detail
—

In a direct election citizens vote directly to choose their representatives or leaders. In an indirect election citizens vote for representatives, who then choose the leaders. Members of the Lok Sabha at the central level, of the Vidhan Sabha at the state level, and of local bodies — Panchayats, municipal corporations and the rest — are elected directly, every five years. The President, the Vice President and members of the Rajya Sabha are elected indirectly.

Six states have a bicameral legislature — Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. There the Lower House is the Vidhan Sabha and the Upper House is the Vidhan Parishad (Legislative Council), made up of members elected by the Vidhan Sabha and by local bodies, and by graduates and teachers in the State — plus members the Governor nominates to represent art, science, social service, literature and co-operatives.

Psephology
The scientific study of elections. From the Greek psēphos, meaning pebble, and logy, systematic study — because in ancient Greece pebbles were what people voted with.
02Why hold one at all?Fig. 7.1 · and three questions the chapter asks30 XP

Pick everything the chapter says about why elections matter — and leave the three it answers with a flat no.

The chapter opens with three questions. Can a class representative elected last year simply continue this year without a fresh election? Can a government continue beyond its term without seeking the people's mandate again? Can we exercise a choice if only one party is contesting? The answer to all three is no — because participating in the periodic election of those who decide on our behalf is one of the most crucial elements of democracy.

Fig. 7.1 hangs four things off elections — equality, representation, accountability and legitimacy — and then leaves two boxes empty for you to fill. What else does an election secure that nothing before it could?

Part 2 · How votes become seats
03Three systems, three countriesHaritbhumi, Ratnadweep and Swarnalok35 XP

The same votes, counted three different ways. Tap each system and watch who ends up governing.

How voting works
—
Who forms the government
—
—

The first step in running an election is deciding how votes cast are turned into seats — and that is what distinguishes one electoral system from another. The framers of our Constitution discussed the two most common systems and chose the plurality system, better known as First-Past-The-Post.

India uses FPTP for the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha. Elections to the Rajya Sabha, and those of the President and Vice President, use proportional representation. So do elections to the Vidhan Parishad, by means of a single transferable vote.

Let's explore
Different democracies use different electoral systems. In a group of five or six, pick six countries from different continents, find out which electoral system each one runs, and look up the results of its most recent election. Does the system seem to change what kind of government comes out?

Notice what the vote shares in Fig. 7.4 do. In Haritbhumi a party with 40 per cent of the votes takes the whole government while 60 per cent of voters backed somebody else. In Ratnadweep the party that led the first round loses the second. In Swarnalok every party's share of the seats matches its share of the votes. Three arithmetics, three different countries.

05The single transferable voteFig. 7.3 · quota, elimination, transfer35 XP

Twelve hundred valid votes and three seats to fill. Work the count one round at a time.

Round
0 of 5
Seats filled
0 of 3
—

Fig. 7.3 gives the procedure in four steps. One: voters mark their preferences. Two: first preference votes are counted for all candidates, and those who reach the minimum votes required to win — the quota — are declared elected. Three: the candidate with the lowest votes is eliminated, and their votes are transferred to whoever is marked as second preference on those ballot papers. Four: the process continues until the required number of candidates are elected.

The quota is the whole trick. Quota = (total valid votes ÷ (seats to be filled + 1)) + 1. It is the smallest number of votes that only as many candidates as there are seats can possibly reach — which is why reaching it settles the matter.

Where these numbers come from
The chapter prints the procedure and the formula, not a worked example. The five candidates and their votes here are an illustration built to follow those rules exactly — so the arithmetic is worth checking against the formula rather than memorising.
06Where the line goesDelimitation, and one MP for twenty-five lakh35 XP

Thirty lakh people, two seats, and one boundary between them. Drag it and watch what each MP ends up representing.

Constituency A
—
Constituency B
—
The gap
—

The boundaries of your parliamentary and assembly constituencies are not permanently fixed. They change over time as population density shifts. Without delimitation one Member of Parliament might represent five lakh people while another represents twenty-five lakh — which defeats the whole object of equal representation.

Delimitation is the process of determining the number of seats and fixing the territorial boundaries in each state for elections to the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha. It aims to keep the ratio of seats to population as close to equal as possible across all constituencies.

Four commissions, and one long gap
Article 82 of the Constitution mandates the establishment of a Delimitation Commission. India has had four — in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002. Twenty-nine years separate the third from the fourth. Find out why, with your teacher.
Part 3 · The rules, and the referee
07Which Act covers this?The Representation of the People Acts, 1950 and 195130 XP

Two Acts, one year apart, and a clean division of labour between them. Sort these eight.

RPA 1950 deals mainly with the allocation of seats and the delimitation of constituencies, the preparation and revision of electoral rolls, and ensuring that every citizen of 18 and above has the right to vote without discrimination. RPA 1951 deals with all the other aspects of the conduct of elections and with post-election disputes: it lays down rules for the nomination of candidates, election campaigns, voting procedures and the resolution of disputes. Together they secure the integrity, transparency and accountability of India's electoral process.

And a third Act
There is also The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 — because the two offices elected indirectly by an electoral college needed rules of their own.
08Offence, or ordinary campaigning?What RPA 1951 lists as a corrupt practice30 XP

Pick every one that RPA 1951 lists as an electoral offence — and leave the three that are simply how a campaign is run.

The Act names three kinds of thing. A gift, offer or promise made by a candidate, or with their consent, to make somebody contest, withdraw, vote, or refrain from voting. An appeal to vote or refrain from voting on the basis of religion, caste, race, community or language. And taking assistance from government-related personnel — gazetted officers, judges and magistrates, armed forces personnel, police personnel and excise officers are all barred from helping a candidate.

Why that third one
The people on that list all hold state power of some kind — a magistrate's authority, a policeman's, an excise officer's. A campaign that can borrow any of it is no longer competing on equal terms with one that cannot.
09What the Commission doesFour jobs, and 96.8 crore voters35 XP

The Constitution vests the superintendence, direction and control of the entire election process in one body. Tap through what that actually means.

The job
—
How it works
—
—

The Election Commission of India is an autonomous permanent constitutional body, established on 25 January 1950. It conducts elections to the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha, the Vidhan Sabha, the Vidhan Parishad, and to the offices of President and Vice President. Articles 324 to 329 of the Constitution provide for it and define its powers and duties.

At the state level the work is supervised by the Chief Electoral Officer, appointed by the ECI from among the civil servants in consultation with the State Government. District Magistrates, Sub-Divisional Magistrates and Tahsildars are assigned election duties as District Election Officers, Returning Officers and Electoral Registration Officers.

No voter to be left behind
The ECI's inclusion work covers Persons with Disabilities, senior citizens, transgender persons and Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups — infrastructure accessibility and technology-assisted inclusion alike. EVMs carry Braille. And voting from home, for senior citizens above 85 and for PwDs with a benchmark disability of 40 per cent, was extended across India for the first time during the 2024 General Elections.
10Added, or deleted?Special Intensive Revision of the electoral roll30 XP

A revision of the roll works in both directions at once. Sort these six.

The ECI sends official enumerators to every household to collect data about eligible electors, and prepares a roll for each constituency, organised polling-station-wise. Only those whose names appear on the roll are allowed to vote.

Special Intensive Revision updates, verifies and corrects those rolls, so that no eligible citizen is left out and no ineligible person is included. It catches the young voters who have just turned 18 and might be missed through a simple lack of awareness. It removes names on the grounds of death, change of residence, duplicate enrolment, or a voter being permanently untraceable. And before the final roll is published, the ECI gives time to raise claims or objections against the revised version, and settles them.

Part 4 · The machinery, and the parties
11Seven apps, three audiencesFig. 7.6 · the digital ecosystem35 XP

Each of these was built for somebody in particular. Tap one and see whose lane it sits in.

Built for
—
What it does
—
—

India's electoral exercise is unparalleled: over 96.8 crore eligible voters spread across diverse regions and terrains, managed autonomously by one Commission. Updating rolls, candidate nominations, regulating campaigns, law enforcement, coordination among states, security arrangements, counting, declaring results and resolving disputes — the ECI runs all of it on information and communication technologies and e-governance.

Beyond the border
The International Election Visitors' Programme is the ECI's flagship programme for cooperation with the Election Management Bodies of other countries. It has signed Memorandums of Understanding with 28 EMBs and three international organisations: the International Foundation for Electoral Systems, International IDEA, and the United Nations.
12National, state, or neither?Fig. 7.12 · the recognition thresholds35 XP

Ten parties, ten results. Slide through them and see which threshold each one clears.

Recognised as
—
Under
—
The condition
—

Only political parties registered with the ECI can contest elections — though independent candidates, affiliated to no party, can contest too. The ECI classifies parties as recognised national parties, recognised state or regional parties, or registered-unrecognised parties. National and state parties are allotted election symbols, and the ECI acts as a quasi-judicial body in disputes over recognition and symbols. It also insists that parties hold their own organisational elections periodically — inner party democracy.

Each list of conditions is an any one of list: a party needs to clear only one of them. A Registered Unrecognised Political Party is one that has not secured enough of the vote in an Assembly or General Election, or has never contested an election at all since registering.

13What a party is forFig. 7.11 · and the two halves of a legislature35 XP

Winning is only one of the two jobs on this diagram. Tap through it.

What happens here
—
Why it matters
—
—

There are often dozens of contestants for each constituency. Most belong to a political party, though some contest independently — and voters learn about candidates, their policies, their vision for development and their positions on social, economic, cultural and political issues primarily through the parties. Fig. 7.9 gives five reasons they are essential: they work directly at the grassroots level, they organise public opinion, they campaign on specific issues, they enable voters to make informed decisions, and they offer voters meaningful choices.

India has a multi-party system: many parties exist and compete, reflecting the country's diversity of languages, cultures, religions and regions.

The era of alliances
1967 ended the era of single-party dominated elections. In 1977, against the backdrop of the National Emergency, several parties formed an alliance as the Janata Party and made the first coalition government at the national level. Since the late 1990s the major alliances have been the National Democratic Alliance, led by the BJP, and the United Progressive Alliance, led by the INC until its dissolution in 2023 and reconstitution as the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance.
Part 5 · Where it strains
14Defection, and the law against it1985, and the 52nd Amendment30 XP

Pick everything the chapter says about defection and the law — and leave the two it does not.

Can someone leave one party and join another whenever they wish? Yes, they can. But once a person has been elected on a particular party's ticket, leaving that party is defection — abandoning or switching from the party under whose banner the candidate was elected. It may mean joining another party, or acting independently of the party's decisions, particularly when voting in the legislature.

The chapter is careful to give both readings. Understood in terms of party discipline and political stability, such actions are political opportunism. Read the other way, defection can be a way of upholding conscience or responding to changed public expectations.

The whip
A party's instruction to its members on how to vote in the House. Under the Anti-Defection Law, voting against it — or voluntarily giving up party membership — can get a member disqualified. The Speaker or Chairman of the House decides what is to be done in such cases.
15The road to a free and fair electionFig. 7.13 · potholes, and what is laid over them35 XP

Fig. 7.13 draws the challenges as potholes in a road, and leaves two of them empty for you to name. Lay the measures the chapter lists and watch the surface.

Measures laid
0 of 5
Last laid
—
—

Conducting elections for over 96.8 crore voters, with thousands of polling stations and hundreds of political parties, across diverse regions and socio-economic realities, is a genuinely difficult task. The chapter names three challenges — misinformation, fake news and intimidation — and then lists what the ECI uses against them: RPA 1950 and 1951, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, the Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail, and voters' awareness campaigns.

Notice that it lists the measures against the challenges as a set, not one against one. No single measure fixes misinformation. What the chapter claims is narrower and more honest: with constant vigilance and active citizen participation, elections can become more representative and the democracy more robust.

The voters' pledge
Every year 25 January is National Voters' Day. The pledge runs: "We, the citizens of India, having abiding faith in democracy, hereby pledge to uphold the democratic traditions of our country and the dignity of free, fair and peaceful elections, and to vote in every election fearlessly and without being influenced by considerations of religion, race, caste, community, language or any inducement."
